1.pericope_label: Nebuchadnezzar the king, unto all people, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth; Peace be multiplied unto you. I thought it good to shew the signs and wonders that the high God hath wrought toward me. How great are his signs! and how mighty are his wonders! his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion is from generation to generation.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch set the chapter out as a proclamation in which the living God of heaven made himself known as ruler over the kingdoms of men. Ellicott places it in the eighteen-year blank at the end of the reign, infers from the address to all the earth that time had passed since the previous chapter, and suspects from the scriptural phrases in the letter that Daniel wrote it at the king's request.

Gill rejects the versions that attach these verses to the preceding chapter, since they preface a dream concerning the king himself, and reads the plain title as the mark of a humbled man without pronouncing the conversion real. Calvin reaches the same division from the shifting persons of the narrative, and explains the chapter as the punishment of a man who had been compelled to confess Israel's God yet never left his own superstitions.

Clarke calls the document a regular decree and one of the most ancient on record, and summarises the whole chapter as a state paper acknowledging God's hand in the king's late malady. Wesley supposes it was lodged in the archives and court rolls, and identifies the greeting as the usual eastern salutation.

Henry notes that the king lays aside the swelling titles he had once used, being old and lately recovered from a distraction that mortified him, holds that he published his own infamy because nobody else would have dared, and turns the greeting into a maxim, that kings should disperse their good wishes with their commands and bless their subjects as fathers of their country.

debates.question: Do these verses belong to the previous chapter or begin this one?

positions.position: They begin this one: the Hebrew and the Greek and Latin versions attach them to what precedes, but they preface a dream concerning the king himself, and the Syriac and Arabic divide rightly.
They begin this one, as appears from the shifting persons: the edict stands in the king's name and other events are inserted, and the roughness of the transitions leaves the sense clear.

debates.question: Who composed the proclamation?

positions.position: Probably Daniel at the king's request, since scriptural phrases appear throughout the letter.
The king himself, who published his own infamy because no one else would have dared, which is why the original paper survives.
A regular decree issued by the king, one of the most ancient on record.

outliers.claim: Holds that nothing less than a real change of heart could produce such a confession from a man of more than forty years' reign who had seen as much of the world as most men ever do.
Locates the chapter in the blank of eighteen years at the end of the reign, whose only known facts are the mania that kept the king under restraint and the later extension of his dominions.

themes: Nebuchadnezzar the king, unto all people, nations, and languages, that dwell in all the earth; Peace be multiplied unto you.
I thought it good to shew the signs and wonders that the high God hath wrought toward me.
How great are his signs! and how mighty are his wonders! his kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and his dominion is from generation to generation.

4.pericope_label: I Nebuchadnezzar was at rest in mine house, and flourishing in my palace: I saw a dream which made me afraid, and the thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head troubled me. Therefore made I a decree to bring in all the wise men of Babylon before me, that they might make known unto me the interpretation of the dream. Then came in the magicians, the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers: and I told the dream before them; but they did not make known unto me the interpretation thereof. But at the last Daniel came in before me, whose name was Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods: and before him I told the dream, saying, O Belteshazzar, master of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in thee, and no secret troubleth thee, tell me the visions of my dream that I have seen, and the interpretation thereof.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch gloss the word for quiet as undisturbed and secure prosperity, note the abrupt introduction of the dream as illustrating the suddenness of the event, and take the word for flourishing from the growth of trees. Ellicott makes the same botanical point and thinks the word was chosen because of the dream that follows, adding that the Greek version dates the chapter to the eighteenth year.

Gill dates the dream by working back through a forty-five-year reign to about the thirty-fifth, and draws the moral that God can make the minds of the greatest men uneasy amid all their glory. Calvin is contemptuous of the wise men, who covered their shamelessness with honourable titles and deluded men with miserable predictions, and takes their failure to prove that the interpretation came by revelation rather than skill; he also reads the Babylonian name given to Daniel as a wound, imposed by the tyrant's cunning to make him forget his family.

Clarke names the conquests that preceded the dream and derives the king's pride and its chastisement directly from them. Wesley puts the same point plainly, that with the wars over he sat down quiet and enjoyed the spoils of his enemies.

Henry dates the dream to the completion of the conquests and explains why the warning was given at all: that when the thing came to pass the king might compare it with the prediction, see it was the Lord's doing, and learn that there is a divine revelation in the world as well as a divine providence.

debates.question: Why did Daniel come in last?

positions.position: By providence, so the magicians might first be seen baffled and Daniel's God the more glorified.
By office: as chief of the governors of the wise men he would not come in until last.
Because the king had settled it that divination, if it existed anywhere, lay with his own men; their failure proves the whole science a fallacy.

debates.question: What does the title master of the magicians concede?

positions.position: Either that he excelled them, though he would have scorned to be counted of their order, or that the king had set him over them.
The spirit of the holy gods means the king's own gods, since he owned a high God only as one among many.
A humiliation on both sides: the king is compelled to venerate a man he had passed over, and the Babylonian name wounds a prophet whose own name marked him a Jew.

outliers.claim: Reads the renaming of Daniel as a deliberate stratagem of the tyrant, meant to render a holy servant of God degenerate by making him forget his own family, so that every use of the Babylonian name offended him.
Notes that the word rendered troubles in the king's request means literally to goad.

themes: I Nebuchadnezzar was at rest in mine house, and flourishing in my palace:
I saw a dream which made me afraid, and the thoughts upon my bed and the visions of my head troubled me.
Therefore made I a decree to bring in all the wise men of Babylon before me, that they might make known unto me the interpretation of the dream.
Then came in the magicians, the astrologers, the Chaldeans, and the soothsayers: and I told the dream before them; but they did not make known unto me the interpretation thereof.
But at the last Daniel came in before me, whose name was Belteshazzar, according to the name of my god, and in whom is the spirit of the holy gods: and before him I told the dream, saying,

O Belteshazzar, master of the magicians, because I know that the spirit of the holy gods is in thee, and no secret troubleth thee, tell me the visions of my dream that I have seen, and the interpretation thereof.

10.pericope_label: Thus were the visions of mine head in my bed; I saw, and behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was great. The tree grew, and was strong, and the height thereof reached unto heaven, and the sight thereof to the end of all the earth: The leaves thereof were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all: the beasts of the field had shadow under it, and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof, and all flesh was fed of it. I saw in the visions of my head upon my bed, and, behold, a watcher and an holy one came down from heaven; He cried aloud, and said thus, Hew down the tree, and cut off his branches, shake off his leaves, and scatter his fruit: let the beasts get away from under it, and the fowls from his branches:

schools.summary: Ellicott names the tree as a common symbol of majesty, cites a Greek historian's report of a similar Persian dream, records that the Greek version has the sun and moon dwelling in the tree and lighting the whole earth, and explains the watcher as a holy one who is watchful, translated angel in one version and merely transliterated in another.

Gill reads each feature politically, the growth as increasing power, the fair leaves as the provinces or their governors, the fruit as what the empire yielded. Calvin grounds the figure in the purpose of government itself, that rulers exist to be trees on whose fruit men feed and under whose shade they rest, so that even tyrants are trees whether they wish it or not; he argues the watchers' title from their nature and defends the roughness of taking a heart from a tree.

Clarke observes that princes are often figured as trees, reports that watchers and holy ones are angels of different orders according to the Chaldean oracles, and reads the flight of the beasts as the desertion of courtiers when the madness appeared. Wesley keeps the watcher simply a holy angel, the instrument of God's judgments.

debates.question: What is a watcher?

positions.position: Angels of two different orders on the Chaldean reckoning, a kind of judges of human actions with power to determine men's lot.
A holy angel, the instrument of God, the angels watching constantly to perform his judgments.
So called from their nature: perpetually awake in performing God's commands, not subject to slumber, having no bodies and so no use for the sleep that follows food and drink.
A holy one who is watchful; the king dreamed in his own mythology and may have thought he saw one of his gods, and is quietly corrected by the prophet, who substitutes the Most High.

debates.question: Why is the tree the right figure for a king?

positions.position: Because government exists for that purpose, rulers being trees on whose fruit all men feed and under whose shadow they rest; even a cruel tyrant is better than no government at all.
Because princes are commonly so represented in the prophets.
Because each feature answers to something in the empire: growth to power, leaves to the provinces, fruit to its yield.

outliers.claim: Dismisses in one breath the notion that Babylon stood at the middle of the earth because it shared a parallel with Jerusalem, calling it foolish, and the older opinion that Jerusalem stood there instead, calling it childish though ancient authors held it.

Argues that the king dreamed in a language and out of an education familiar to him, so that by his own mythology he may have witnessed the descent of one of his deities, and that the prophet corrects him by ascribing the decree to the one true God.

themes: Thus were the visions of mine head in my bed; I saw, and behold a tree in the midst of the earth, and the height thereof was great.
The tree grew, and was strong, and the height thereof reached unto heaven, and the sight thereof to the end of all the earth:

The leaves thereof were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all: the beasts of the field had shadow under it, and the fowls of the heaven dwelt in the boughs thereof, and all flesh was fed of it.
I saw in the visions of my head upon my bed, and, behold, a watcher and an holy one came down from heaven;
He cried aloud, and said thus, Hew down the tree, and cut off his branches, shake off his leaves, and scatter his fruit: let the beasts get away from under it, and the fowls from his branches:

15.pericope_label: Nevertheless leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth: Let his heart be changed from man’s, and let a beast’s heart be given unto him; and let seven times pass over him. This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men. This dream I king Nebuchadnezzar have seen. Now thou, O Belteshazzar, declare the interpretation thereof, forasmuch as all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known unto me the interpretation: but thou art able; for the spirit of the holy gods is in thee.

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the stump as just so much left as could throw up a new sapling, denies that the band means a confined king's chains rather than trouble and affliction, argues at length that the king was probably confined in a court of his palace rather than wandering at large, and refuses to fix the seven times as years, holding that some definite period marked by the heavenly bodies is meant.

Gill takes the stump as continuance in a forlorn condition with hope of restoration, and glosses the changed heart as changed in quality and not in substance; he makes the watchers approvers of the decree rather than its authors, assessors called into consultation after the manner of men. Calvin finds in the stump the specimen of clemency in the whole punishment, and reads the passage as confirming that the sentence cannot be escaped.

Clarke puts the stump in a line, that the king is not to be destroyed nor his kingdom alienated, reads the seven times as seven years, and adds a case of his own acquaintance who believed himself a bear; on the Most High ruling he insists that God never leaves the world's government to men, to second causes or to chance, and that the throne ennobles nobody. Wesley divides the decree from the demand, the one God's and the other the angels', and turns the clause against the flatterers who had allowed the king to be a god on earth.

debates.question: How long are the seven times?

positions.position: Seven years.
Uncertain: the appeal to another passage for years is purely conjectural, and some definite period marked out by the heavenly bodies is likelier.

debates.question: What part do the watchers have in the decree?

positions.position: Approvers and executants, not authors; assessors called into consultation on the analogy of a privy council, though nothing of the sort properly belongs to God.
The decree is God's and the demand the angels', who consent to a just judgment put into their hands.
The request belongs to the holy one and the execution to the watcher.

debates.question: Was the king at large during his madness?

positions.position: Highly improbable: the loyalty of courtiers who never set another man on the throne suggests he was confined in some court of his palace.
He forsook society for the woods and deserts, as in a comparable case of a man who believed himself a bear.

outliers.claim: Quotes a modern writer for the thought that the watchers' part gives a glimpse into the interest of the holy angels in ourselves: they longed that oppression should cease and prayed for the chastisement that would relieve the oppressed and convert the oppressor.
Illustrates the setting up of the basest of men from two successive rulers of his own country, one of whom nearly ruined it in civil and religious matters and the other was the means of restoring it.

themes: Nevertheless leave the stump of his roots in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts in the grass of the earth:
Let his heart be changed from man’s, and let a beast’s heart be given unto him; and let seven times pass over him.

This matter is by the decree of the watchers, and the demand by the word of the holy ones: to the intent that the living may know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will, and setteth up over it the basest of men.

This dream I king Nebuchadnezzar have seen. Now thou, O Belteshazzar, declare the interpretation thereof, forasmuch as all the wise men of my kingdom are not able to make known unto me the interpretation: but thou art able; for the spirit of the holy gods is in thee.

19.pericope_label: Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was astonied for one hour, and his thoughts troubled him. The king spake, and said, Belteshazzar, let not the dream, or the interpretation thereof, trouble thee. Belteshazzar answered and said, My lord, the dream be to them that hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies. The tree that thou sawest, which grew, and was strong, whose height reached unto the heaven, and the sight thereof to all the earth; Whose leaves were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all; under which the beasts of the field dwelt, and upon whose branches the fowls of the heaven had their habitation: It is thou, O king, that art grown and become strong: for thy greatness is grown, and reacheth unto heaven, and thy dominion to the end of the earth.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch describe how the interpretation proceeds, repeating the substance of the dream in abbreviated form before declaring its reference to the king. Ellicott corrects the measure of the silence to a moment rather than an hour, notices the abbreviation as the reverse of what happened with the earlier dream, and measures the empire from Armenia to the Persian Gulf, adding that the king's sin was to want the whole image gold and himself to be the image.

Gill locates the difficulty not in the dream, which was plain to Daniel, but in the shocking things it portended, so that he sat thunderstruck and silent. Calvin turns the prophet's respectfulness into a rule for ministers and calls it the hardest middle course to keep, and explains why a man might grieve for such a king, since the exiles were bound to pray for Babylon's prosperity until the seventy years were out.

Clarke says the prophet was not puzzled by any obscurity but felt the delicacy of the thing for the king and the nation. Wesley admires the short preface as showing address and an excellent spirit, and reckons the empire's extent by its northern, western and southern seas.

Henry gives two causes for the silence at once, terror at so great a judgment on so great a prince, so that his flesh trembled for fear of God, and confusion at having to bring heavy tidings to a man from whom he had received many favours.

debates.question: Why was Daniel silent?

positions.position: Not from any difficulty in the dream, which was plain to him, but from the shocking things it portended.
Not puzzled by obscurity but feeling the delicacy of the message for king and nation.
From terror at the judgment and confusion at having to deliver it to a benefactor.
From sorrow at the punishment, a grief proper to a subject bound to pray for the king he lived under.

debates.question: How should the prophet's opening courtesy be read?

positions.position: A delicate way of expressing his hopes for the best, wishing on the king's enemies what the interpretation implies.
As showing address and an excellent spirit in a very short preface.
As the middle course between fulminating zeal and perfidious flattery, the hardest thing for a minister of the word to keep.

outliers.claim: Warns against two opposite failures in ministers: those who always fulminate under a pretence of zeal, forgetting they are men and showing no benevolence, so that their admonitions are merely hated; and those perfidious flatterers who gloss over the grossest iniquities and cite the prophets as though zeal had driven out all human feeling.
Connects the height of the tree with the earlier vision, in which this king had been the golden head of an image: his sin was to want the whole image gold and himself to be the image.

themes: Then Daniel, whose name was Belteshazzar, was astonied for one hour, and his thoughts troubled him. The king spake, and said, Belteshazzar, let not the dream, or the interpretation thereof, trouble thee. Belteshazzar answered and said, My lord, the dream be to them that hate thee, and the interpretation thereof to thine enemies.
The tree that thou sawest, which grew, and was strong, whose height reached unto the heaven, and the sight thereof to all the earth;
Whose leaves were fair, and the fruit thereof much, and in it was meat for all; under which the beasts of the field dwelt, and upon whose branches the fowls of the heaven had their habitation:
It is thou, O king, that art grown and become strong: for thy greatness is grown, and reacheth unto heaven, and thy dominion to the end of the earth.

23.pericope_label: And whereas the king saw a watcher and an holy one coming down from heaven, and saying, Hew the tree down, and destroy it; yet leave the stump of the roots thereof in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven times pass over him; This is the interpretation, O king, and this is the decree of the most High, which is come upon my lord the king: That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. And whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the tree roots; thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule. Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor; if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity.

schools.summary: Ellicott explains that a third person plural active verb with an impersonal subject regularly stands for a second person singular passive, so the sentence means thou shalt be driven; he renders the promise of the kingdom literally shall arise, meaning that no successor should be appointed during the king's life, and rejects outright the rendering redeem thy sins by alms as unwarranted by the Chaldee. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the structure of the address.

Gill canvasses who the drivers might be and settles on God, perhaps by angels or by the king's own imagination, and notices the delicacy of a servant asking a king to take advice in good part. Calvin notes that interpreters differ even over whether the first word means my counsel or my king, and reads the second as breaking off sin by pity and humanity, so that cruelty is changed into clemency.

Clarke fills in the history, that no new king was set up and the king's son acted as regent during the insanity, and keeps the counsel as a plain imperative to do justice, since the king had been oppressive and should show mercy to the poor he had himself made poor. Wesley calls the speech such a thundering peal that it is wonderful the king endured it, and observes how hard the lesson is for lofty princes.

debates.question: How should the counsel about sins be rendered?

positions.position: Break off, on the metaphor of a refractory beast casting off the yoke; the Chaldee conveys neither alms nor redeeming, so redeem thy sins by alms is incorrect and unwarrantable.
Break off or abolish, by pity and humanity, so that an end is made of sin and tyrannical violence gives way to clemency.
Do justice: the king had been oppressive and must show mercy to the poor he had made poor.

debates.question: Who drives the king from men?

positions.position: Nobody in particular: the active plural stands for a passive, so the words mean thou shalt be driven.
God, and not the family or the nobles, perhaps by ministering angels or by the king's own imagination, judging himself a beast.

debates.question: What is the force of the plural in they commanded?

positions.position: It shows the watchers form a council in which one acts on behalf of all, since the dream ascribed the command to one only.

outliers.claim: Marks the effect the speech should have had, calling it such a thundering peal that it is wonderful the king endured it without fury boiling in him, and observing how hard it is for lofty princes to learn the lesson.
Supplies the history behind the promise that the kingdom would be sure: no new king was set up, and the king's son acted as regent through his father's insanity.

themes: And whereas the king saw a watcher and an holy one coming down from heaven, and saying, Hew the tree down, and destroy it; yet leave the stump of the roots thereof in the earth, even with a band of iron and brass, in the tender grass of the field; and let it be wet with the dew of heaven, and let his portion be with the beasts of the field, till seven times pass over him;
This is the interpretation, O king, and this is the decree of the most High, which is come upon my lord the king:

That they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field, and they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and they shall wet thee with the dew of heaven, and seven times shall pass over thee, till thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.
And whereas they commanded to leave the stump of the tree roots; thy kingdom shall be sure unto thee, after that thou shalt have known that the heavens do rule.
Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor; if it may be a lengthening of thy tranquillity.

28.pericope_label: All this came upon the king Nebuchadnezzar. At the end of twelve months he walked in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon. The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty? While the word was in the king’s mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, saying, O king Nebuchadnezzar, to thee it is spoken; The kingdom is departed from thee. And they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field: they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and seven times shall pass over thee, until thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will. The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch answer the critics who take the third-person narrative as proof that someone other than the king framed the edict, arguing that the first person returns later so the change has its reason in the matter itself, and refusing the explanation that he thought it unbecoming to speak of his own madness. Ellicott dates the twelve months from the vision, gives the dimensions and buildings of the city, insists the palace was the one in Babylon itself, and names the malady as the mania called lycanthropy.

Gill dates the year and reports the fulfilment as real history rather than parable, and denies that any change of nature occurred, since a man turned into a beast would not be the same person and so not the one punished. Calvin refuses to read the twelve months as evidence of repentance deferring the stroke, holding that God withdrew his hand for a year and that the delay made the pride less excusable.

Clarke describes the man in the woods with hair grown thick for clothing and nails hooked for grubbing roots, and calls that clothing a mercy; on the boast he says the heart was inflated and the king acknowledged God in nothing. Wesley admires the propriety of the change of person and glosses the driving as the flight of a distracted man to the woods.

debates.question: Why does the narrative shift to the third person?

positions.position: Not because another hand framed the edict, since the first person returns later; the reason lies in the matter itself, and not in any reluctance to speak of his own madness.
It is common usage among Hebrews and Chaldeans, and the prophet gives the substance of the king's words rather than the words.
It is admirably proper, six verses in the third person and the first resumed as soon as reason returns.

debates.question: Were the twelve months a space granted for repentance?

positions.position: Yes: sufficient time for repentance was mercifully granted.
Either given for repentance or gained by the king's attending a while to the advice.
No: it is improbable the king was touched at all; God withdrew his hand for a year, which made the pride less excusable.

debates.question: What was the nature of the malady?

positions.position: The form of mania called lycanthropy, in which consciousness was retained.
A madness that drove him to the woods, where hair and nails served him as covering and tools.
No change of nature at all: body and mind were severely altered while the essential parts of a man remained, since a beast could not be the person punished.

outliers.claim: Argues from the palace being the one in Babylon itself, with the king at the centre of his dominions, that there is no need to suppose the account written by somebody living far from the city.
Grants that God sometimes indulges the reprobate when he sees them humbled, citing a king spared without repenting cordially, but denies that this is what the year's delay means here.

themes: All this came upon the king Nebuchadnezzar.
At the end of twelve months he walked in the palace of the kingdom of Babylon.
The king spake, and said, Is not this great Babylon, that I have built for the house of the kingdom by the might of my power, and for the honour of my majesty?
While the word was in the king’s mouth, there fell a voice from heaven, saying, O king Nebuchadnezzar, to thee it is spoken; The kingdom is departed from thee.

And they shall drive thee from men, and thy dwelling shall be with the beasts of the field: they shall make thee to eat grass as oxen, and seven times shall pass over thee, until thou know that the most High ruleth in the kingdom of men, and giveth it to whomsoever he will.

The same hour was the thing fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar: and he was driven from men, and did eat grass as oxen, and his body was wet with the dew of heaven, till his hairs were grown like eagles’ feathers, and his nails like birds’ claws.

34.pericope_label: And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High, and I praised and honoured him that liveth for ever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom is from generation to generation: And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?

schools.summary: Ellicott explains that the understanding meant is the sense of personality rather than consciousness, and argues from the psalm-like language of the doxology that the king can hardly have been so versed in the Hebrew scriptures, which supports the conjecture that Daniel composed the letter. Keil and Delitzsch mark the inward connection between the return of reason and the restoration of the throne.

Gill dates the recovery and reckons the remaining year of the reign, and qualifies the clause about men being nothing, since in themselves they are something, their souls immaterial and immortal and worth more than the world, and only comparatively nothing. Calvin takes the seven years' delay as showing how long it takes to cure pride once it has entered the marrow, and weighs the disputed word in the verse, rejecting the harsher reading for the received one.

Wesley says God shone on the king's soul and gave him understanding to consider his sad state and its causes, and lists the senses in which the creature is nothing: nothing to help, nothing to hurt, nothing in duration, nothing without dependence on God.

Henry sets the picture of a man who looked no longer down as a beast but up as a man, and more than that as a penitent, and draws the reckoning that those may justly be counted void of understanding who do not bless God, since men never rightly use their reason until they begin to be religious.

debates.question: What does the returning understanding consist in?

positions.position: Not consciousness so much as the sense of personality, which had been lost for a time.
God shining on the soul and giving him understanding to consider his state and its causes.
Reason restored so far that he glorifies God; men never rightly use their reason until they begin to be religious.

debates.question: In what sense are the inhabitants of the earth nothing?

positions.position: Comparatively only: in themselves men are something, their souls immaterial and immortal and worth more than the whole world.
In several distinct senses at once: nothing to help, nothing to hurt, nothing in duration, nothing solid, nothing without dependence on God.
As the necessary contrast to God's eternity, which all confess in words while few weigh their own frailty.

outliers.claim: Argues from the psalm-like and prophetic language of the doxologies that the king can hardly have been versed enough in the Hebrew scriptures to use them so, which supports the conjecture that Daniel and not the king composed the letter.

Takes the seven years before the king raised his eyes as showing how long it takes to cure pride, since a vital part once corrupt heals slowly and pride that has entered the marrow is not easily plucked out.

themes: And at the end of the days I Nebuchadnezzar lifted up mine eyes unto heaven, and mine understanding returned unto me, and I blessed the most High, and I praised and honoured him that liveth for ever, whose dominion is an everlasting dominion, and his kingdom is from generation to generation:

And all the inhabitants of the earth are reputed as nothing: and he doeth according to his will in the army of heaven, and among the inhabitants of the earth: and none can stay his hand, or say unto him, What doest thou?

36.pericope_label: At the same time my reason returned unto me; and for the glory of my kingdom, mine honour and brightness returned unto me; and my counsellors and my lords sought unto me; and I was established in my kingdom, and excellent majesty was added unto me. Now I Nebuchadnezzar praise and extol and honour the King of heaven, all whose works are truth, and his ways judgment: and those that walk in pride he is able to abase.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch render the two attributes truth and judgment and agree that the king recognised his humiliation as a righteous punishment for pride, while reporting the conclusion that he was never brought to true heart-repentance. Ellicott declines to settle the question and traces instead a progress through the king's successive confessions, ending with the possibility that he had let much of his old belief go and was advancing towards the truth.

Gill has the king now knowing that the heavens rule and giving his praise in the most public way, by word and by writing under his own hand. Calvin makes the restoration a kind of new creation, since a man formed again out of a beast, and hears inside the thanksgiving a confession of fault, the king applying to himself what is said of the proud and owning that no lighter remedy could have arrested his haughtiness.

Clarke thinks it very probable the king was a true convert who relapsed no more and died in the faith of the God of Israel. Wesley challenges the contrary opinion directly, asking what authority anyone had to say this man was no convert, and holds the doxology to proceed from the heart.

debates.question: Was Nebuchadnezzar truly converted?

positions.position: No: he says nothing of the grace shown him, and was never brought to true heart-repentance.
Very probably yes: he relapsed no more into idolatry and died in the faith of the God of Israel.
Yes, and the contrary opinion has no authority: we can no more doubt his salvation than Solomon's, the doxology proceeding from the heart.
Undecided: a progress can be traced through his successive confessions, and this thanksgiving makes it possible that he was advancing towards the truth if not already in possession of it.

debates.question: What is the force of the closing doxology?

positions.position: Public praise from a man who now knows the heavens rule, given by word before his lords and by writing under his own hand.
A confession of fault as much as a thanksgiving: he applies to himself what is said of the proud, God having made him a monument for the instruction of mankind.

outliers.claim: Suggests that the king's hiding place had probably never been discovered, and that providence had so ordered matters that on his return he found his counsellors and lords ready to receive him gladly and serve him as before.

Reconstructs how the king would have been treated during his illness on the Babylonian theory of sickness, supposing himself under an evil spirit and dosed by his magicians with charms, amulets, exorcisms and images of his gods.
